title: ⭐⭐ Revision: who forces, who allows, who arranges

questions.prompt: Two mothers describe the same Saturday. Mother A says: "I let my son cook the lunch." Mother B says: "I made my son cook the lunch." What is the difference between the two?

options.text: A gave an order, B gave permission.
A gave permission, B gave an order.
A cooked the lunch with her son, B did not.
A asked politely, B asked twice.

questions.explanation: let is the verb of permission and make is the verb of obligation, so the difference is that "A gave permission, B gave an order." "A gave an order, B gave permission." swaps the two verbs round. "A cooked the lunch with her son, B did not." invents a second cook: in both sentences the son does the cooking and the mother does not touch it. "A asked politely, B asked twice." turns a difference of meaning into a difference of tone, and neither sentence says how politely or how often anybody asked.

questions.prompt: Read this line from a letter to a magazine: "I told my mother that a friend had upset me, and by the evening the whole family was discussing it as if it were a disaster." Which expression of the lesson describes what her family did?

options.text: They did not see eye to eye with her at all.
They barged into her room without knocking.
They could not help it.
They blew the problem out of proportion.

questions.explanation: To blow a problem out of proportion is to treat something small as if it were huge, and a whole family debating one upset as a disaster is exactly that, so the answer is "They blew the problem out of proportion." "They barged into her room without knocking." means entering rudely, and nobody enters anywhere in this scene. "They did not see eye to eye with her at all." means they disagreed with her, but the family is never said to disagree, only to exaggerate. "They could not help it." means they were unable to stop themselves, which the line does not tell us either.

questions.prompt: A pupil has filled in this chart of who does what at home: "handling the family finances every month — mother · ironing the school shirts every Sunday — father · comforting whoever has had a bad week — grandmother · enforcing the rules about screens — mother". Only one of these four roles is affective. Which one?

options.text: handling the family finances every month
ironing the school shirts every Sunday
comforting whoever has had a bad week
enforcing the rules about screens

questions.explanation: An affective role works on feelings — comfort, warmth, reassurance — so "comforting whoever has had a bad week" is the one. "handling the family finances every month" belongs to the maintenance and management of the family system, which is instrumental. "ironing the school shirts every Sunday" is a practical chore, instrumental too, however loving the person who does it. "enforcing the rules about screens" is discipline, and discipline is filed on the instrumental side with decision making and standards.

questions.prompt: In which pair do the letters "ou" stand for the same sound?

options.text: cousin / young
cousin / house
house / young
through / cousin

questions.explanation: In "cousin / young" the letters ou say the same short vowel in both words, the one you hear in but and son. In "cousin / house" the second word opens on the vowel of now, which cousin does not have. In "house / young" those two different vowels sit one in each word, so the pair differs as well. In "through / cousin" the ou of through is the long vowel of food, again a different sound. The spelling is identical in all four words and the sound is not: that is the whole point of the exercise.

questions.prompt: A pupil hands in these four sentences about housework at home. Three of them are correct English. Which one must be corrected?

options.text: My father wants us to plan the week together on Sunday evening.
He makes my brother and me to write our tasks on the board.
My mother has my sister water the plants before school.
If a family shares the housework, nobody is overburdened.

questions.explanation: "He makes my brother and me to write our tasks on the board." is the faulty one: after make plus its object the verb keeps its base form, so it must read makes my brother and me write. The to belongs to want alone. "My father wants us to plan the week together on Sunday evening." is correct for that very reason: want does take the person and then a to-infinitive. "My mother has my sister water the plants before school." is correct too — has here is the causative, not the auxiliary of a perfect tense, and it means the mother arranges for the sister to do the watering. "If a family shares the housework, nobody is overburdened." is correct because an automatic result keeps a present tense in both halves.

questions.prompt: Read this letter to a magazine. "I am seventeen. My father checks my marks every evening and asks me the same three questions. He never tells me he is proud of me, but last week I heard him tell a neighbour that I would go far. I wish he would say it to my face." What is the writer's main complaint?

options.text: Her father does not believe that she will succeed.
Her father takes no interest in her school results.
Her father keeps his approval for other people.
Her father forbids her to speak to the neighbours.

questions.explanation: Her father praises her to a neighbour and never to her, and her last sentence asks for precisely that, so the complaint is "Her father keeps his approval for other people." "Her father does not believe that she will succeed." contradicts the very words she overheard, in which he says she will go far. "Her father takes no interest in her school results." is the opposite of a man who checks the marks every single evening. "Her father forbids her to speak to the neighbours." invents a ban that the letter never mentions at all.
